claims.text: An asset is an item of value that a business owns and expects to use in its operations or turn into cash; assets are classified as non-current assets, kept for use for more than one year, and current assets, expected to be used, sold or turned into cash within a year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A liability is a debt a business owes to an outside party; current liabilities, such as trade payables and a bank overdraft, fall due for payment within a year, while non-current liabilities, such as a long-term bank loan, fall due after more than a year.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The one-year test sorts assets and liabilities: an item the business expects to use, sell or pay within a year is current, and an item kept or owed beyond a year is non-current; a delivery van kept for the business's own deliveries is a non-current asset, while the same van held for resale is part of inventories, a current asset.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Trade receivables are amounts owed to a business by customers who bought on credit, so they are a current asset; trade payables are amounts the business owes to its suppliers, so they are a current liability - the direction of the debt is what separates them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A statement of financial position shows the assets a business owns, the liabilities it owes and the capital invested by its owners at one point in time - a snapshot of what the business owns and owes on that date, unlike the income statement, which reports performance over a period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A reader can deduce from a statement of financial position how the business is financing its activities - the share of funds from the owners' capital, from long-term borrowing and from short-term credit - and what assets it owns, both the long-term resources and the short-term items moving through the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Selling inventories raises finance from inside the business, because goods already held pass to buyers and their value arrives as cash; sold in a hurry, the goods may fetch less than their usual price and the lines are no longer available to sell, so the relief is one-off rather than a lasting source of funds.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Comparing current assets with current liabilities shows whether a business is likely to be able to pay its short-term debts: a margin of current assets over current liabilities suggests a comfortable position, while current liabilities above current assets suggest pressure on the business's short-term payments.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
